html:
Norman Tindale was an Australian anthropologist and entomologist at the South Australian Museum, best known for mapping the territories of Aboriginal Australian peoples as they were at the time of European contact.

He joined the museum in 1918 to work on insects. On a trip to Groote Eylandt in 1921 and 1922 he began recording Aboriginal languages, kinship and land, and over the next fifty years he travelled widely across Australia doing the same. His book Aboriginal Tribes of Australia (1974) came with a map of tribal boundaries for the whole continent.

The map is still the starting point for most work on where Aboriginal peoples lived, and for many small groups, such as the Kalaako and Malpa, the Agwamin and the Limilngan, it is the main record. It has also been criticised for drawing fixed lines around peoples whose boundaries were often more fluid, and some of his groupings, as with the Wuthathi, are disputed.
